claims.text: The initial NbMoTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous single-phase BCC structure.
A short anneal at approximately 900 °C followed by rapid quenching will nucleate Laves-phase nanoprecipitates in NbMoTaW-based alloys.
Optimized time-temperature control will produce a uniform population of fine, coherent Laves-phase nanoprecipitates.
Irradiation at approximately 700 °C simulates the relevant plasma-facing operational environment.
Coherent Laves-phase interfaces absorb irradiation-induced dislocation loops and vacancy clusters.
Absorption of irradiation defects at precipitate interfaces enhances defect recombination and produces a self-healing microstructure.
The proposed precipitate structure prevents uncontrolled accumulation of irradiation defects.
The precipitate-mediated mechanism mitigates radiation swelling.
The heat-treated alloy will preserve or modestly enhance yield strength after irradiation.
The heat-treated alloy will preserve or modestly enhance ductility after irradiation.
The treatment will reduce irradiation-induced defect density by approximately 20% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will reduce radiation swelling by approximately 20% relative to the untreated alloy.
Untreated NbMoTaW-based alloy irradiated under the same conditions will exhibit higher defect density and swelling than the treated alloy.
The beneficial effect is limited to irradiation near 700 °C and a finely controlled heat-treatment profile.
Departure from the optimized heat-treatment profile can produce nonuniform or coarsened precipitates.
Nonuniform or coarsened precipitates can cause localized embrittlement or degraded mechanical performance.
